messages.subject: Dispersal movements and CTMM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

first of all thanks for the contents presented on the last Webinar which clarified a lot some remained doubts I had before. I am very glad to see the improvements in CTMM and It is very enjoyable work with this tool for telemetry analysis. Now, I'm becoming a little bit more confident and fluent with CTMM. As a consequence, new challenges and new doubts are raising.

My first question: I have some Pumas samples with a well featured dispersal movement at the beginning of the data sample, after past a few months the animal established Its home range area very far away from the initial point of the track. As the full data sample contain two distinct movements, should I split the data in two sub datasets and treat these movements separately? I found one paper about "Marcher" package, you are there, but I felt that "Marcher" has the main focus on migratory movement and home range shifts, may I wrong in this interpretation? My concern is do all the process taking in account auto-correlation and avoid an arbitrary cut to separate both movements. Also, during last webinar someone told something about the cluster package named "SegClust2D". I took a look at the paper of this package and I identified clear differences between "marcher" and "segclust2D" approach, something like BICxHMM (Bayesian Information Criterion X Hidden Markov Models), worse, I visited the segclust2D homepage and browsed through Its vignette, which seems to be more easy to understand and run into R than "marcher". Now, I am a bit more confused about what is the best choice to work with this kind of data properly and keep on working with my analysis in companion of CTMM? Again I find my self in a human uncertainty field, because sometimes "easy" could be mean hard. :-)

The second question: You told, in webinar, that occurrence function only shows up the uncertainty around points where animal walked through in the past. If I'll use occurrence map yielded by CTMM to overlap areas where animal walked through against a land-use map to validate animal habitat and space preferences, could be It a mistaken use of occurrence map and occurrence function?

Third question: CTMM Overlap function only calculates animals overlaps? Or could be possible calculates overlaps between animal space used and land use area (forested, agricultural and anthropized areas)?

Fourth question: There is some paper or vignette about Speed function? I am facing some problems to make this function runs out of the box properly with my samples.

Five question: When variogram shows up a not resident movement for any animal, should I either jump out of analysis or go to the next step and apply the Fit function? I am asking that because I already ran this task with this heterogeneous dataset (home range and dispersal movement together) and It took a long time to finish the calculations and bring the summary outputs, almost a entire day. To produce a more realistic results from the others CTMM functions (speed(s), occurrence...) It is always necessary Fits the model before under any circumstances, right?

Best regards,

Sergio.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sergio,

If you want to do range estimation, then you will want to segment your data. Segmentation is an open problem, but I have heard good reports about segclust2D. It does not account for autocorrelation, but has a very robust/exhaustive algorithm for detecting the change points.
I think that's a valid use. I would take expectation values by exporting the PMF.
As with (2), you would want to calculate expectation values with the exported PMF. For instance, sum(PMF*NDVI) gives you the (point estimate of) mean NDVI value that the animal sampled during the observation period.
https://movementecologyjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40462-019-0177-1
I'm not exactly sure what you are asking, but such a model could potentially be okay for speed() and occurrence(), where consistent short-lag behavior is more critical, though it wouldn't be okay for akde().

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: home range estimation in the presence of barriers or non-used areas
messages.subject_clean: home range estimation in the presence of barriers or non-used areas
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I am fitting ctmm to some animal trajectories and estimating home range area and movement parameters within that. The idea is to relate the HR area and these parameters (speed, autocorrelation times) with mean values of environmental covariates extracted for each 95% akde isopleth.

However, in my case several animals are living in the borders of a dam, which they do not use and do not cross. When I look at the akde polygon it takes a great part of the dam, even though this area of water is not used for e.g. foraging, mating, conspecific attraction or avoidance (as the classical definitions of home range). It may be a barrier to movement, and influence habitat selection, though. Here below there is an example of an individual, and we see the water comprises a great part of the HR, even though the animal is restricted to a "peninsula".

This question could be extended to other kinds of barriers, I guess. How to deal with home range size calculation and extraction of covariates? Should I remove the area of the dam (and beyond) to calculate these quantities?

I know this is not a new a topic and also arises for other home range estimators, such as traditional KDEs. There is this study by Benhamou and Cornélis 2010 that accounts for barriers in KDE, and I found some other approaches, but nothing related to ctmm and akde. And it seems to me that generally akde's polygons are larger than other estimators HRs, potentially including more barriers or other places where movement is restricted or not possible.

Does anyone has experience on how to deal with these cases?

Best wishes,
Bernardo

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bernardo,

Yeah, KDEs have discontinuity bias where they spill over boundaries and convex hull methods are only ensured to respect convex boundaries (e.g., not winding rivers).

The simplest solution is to mask the CDF. The AKDE's grid coordinates are located in AKDE$r$x and AKDE$r$y and the CDF is in AKDE$CDF. So, you can just loop over the rows (i) and columns (j) of the CDF like

for(i in 1:nrow(AKDE$CDF)) {
  for(j in 1:ncol(AKDE$CDF)) {
    if( c(AKDE$r$x[i],AKDE$r$y[j]) is an inaccessible location )
    { AKDE$CDF[i,j] <- 1 }
}}

Then when you calculate the home range areas of the AKDE, those regions will not be included.

A slightly better solution is to mask the individual kernels, as Benhamou and Cornélis sugges, but I haven't coded this up yet.

Even better is to to also mask at the autocorrelation model fitting stage, with a non-linear filter. This is all some time out.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Minimum number of locations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sharon,

There is a lot of information on the required amount of data in https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13270

There isn't a minimum number of points per se (unless the data are IID), but more a minimum number of observed range crossings, which is also dependent on the estimator being used and the tolerance for bias. Often times with IID VHF data, people are surprised when I tell them that their 20 locations are worth more than a year of Mongolian gazelle data. Variograms can be hard to look at when there isn't much data, so you might try pooling individuals with the mean() function ( https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/mean.variogram.html ).

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: AKDE and KDE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Malena,

I'm not exactly clear on the question. You want to know why your ctmm KDE (not AKDE?) estimates are different from the adehabitat KDE estimates (using the above code)? There are many possible differences here:
adehabitat's "href" bandwidth optimizer is the rule-of-thumb method, while ctmm's IID bandwidth optimizer is the GRF method. Neither of these is really better than the other and they should be pretty close for large n.
adehabitat's kernel and reference covariance is circular, while ctmm's kernel and reference covariance may be circular or elliptical, depending on which model is selected (isotropic or anisotropic). Elliptical can be preferable for animals with elongated home ranges, but often times it's not a big difference.
By default, ctmm applies a GRF bias correction to both the AKDE and KDE areas ( https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12673 ). This can yield a big improvement for small n.
If the data are autocorrelated, AKDE can be much larger (with much more uncertainty) than KDE from either package.
If the data have substantial location error (and you model that), then the ctmm AKDEs and KDEs will shrink appropriately.
Does this answer your question?

Best,
Chris

To estimate speed/distance, you need the sampling rate to be high enough that there is some persistence of velocity between fixes. There can be some gaps, but there needs to be some finer scale data too. Daily sampling can be adequate for a global migration, but would not be good enough for most range resident ungulates.

Best,
Chris

I have been working my way through the vignettes to estimate home ranges of bilbies I have GPS tracking data for (nocturnal, burrowing marsupials).

I was really impressed at how easy it was to learn the basic workflows for ctmm from the paper in Methods in Ecology and Evolution - a great paper, thank you!

Thanks in advance.

Kind regards,
Cass

messages.subject: Re: AKDE and cyclical fix schedule
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cass,

Rather than applying an HDOP threshold, I would recommend taking your stationary testing data and using that to select an error model and calibrating your tracking data: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.06.12.130195v1
At scales this small, a good error model could potentially have some impact on your estimates.

1. If these are nocturnal data and you are only sampling at night, then you don't need to apply AKDE weights. In fact, if your data starts and ends at the burrows, then the weights are going to bias towards the burrows, because the model doesn't know that the start/end times are any different from the midnight times.

Hi Cass,

CI="Gauss" requires better data quality than the default setting (because it has to reference the semi-variance at smaller lags to estimate the CIs at larger lags) and it looks like it isn't going to be able to cooperate with the gaps in your data. I would go back to what you were doing. Sorry about that.

I'm not familiar with fitted.models(). What package is that from? I would go with the selected model, though those look pretty similar.

Those model fits look to be a little bit above the empirical variograms, though not as much as the end of the first plot you shared. That could be from a mild amount of range shifting or it could be bias from the location error not being modeled yet.

The first thing I would do is to model the error and calibrate your tracking data. If you calculate your variogram from calibrated data with fast=FALSE, then that also improves the quality of the variogram (for data with relatively large location errors). Your 1-day ranges appear to be ~5-10 hectares (200-300 meters)^2, and GPS location errors tend to be 10-100 meters, and possibly more of the latter with a burrowing species. Given that those scales are similar, you can get substantial bias in both the empirical variograms and the fitted models, if you don't model the error.

If you still see the discrepancy, then I would consider trying to either segment the data (if that appears possible), which is more for animals that shift their range suddenly, or doing a windowed analysis if the range shifting is more continuous. Armadillos tend to move around a network of burrows and often need the latter. In the future, we will have more complex models that can incorporate random range shifts like.

Best,
Chris
